The Case for Investigating IDWT's Sector Structure

Updated October 9, 2026

Abstract

Can the spatial dimensionality of a particle's wave pattern organize its frequency, rotation properties and interaction? Infinite Dimensional Wave Theory (IDWT) proposes one field on nested ordinary spatial sectors, with particle mass-frequencies proportional to a simplex count. The maintained electron–muon ratio misses its archived benchmark by about 17.3 parts per million, whereas neighboring muon indices change the ratio by 15–17%. Under the stated absolute scale prescription, shared charged-lepton unit and exclusive occupied depths, only the maintained complete arrangement reaches every existing individual mass accuracy, even allowing every positive integer index. At those same proposed depths, explicit geometry constrains further properties: common six-/ten-dimensional spatial spectral families realize the target count polynomials and contain observer half-spin states; two conditional channel criteria give rank three only at the quark depths three and four; depth five supplies a shared handedness and neutral-generator construction. A compatible normal geometry links charge weights, polarization frames, spin sections and contact, while separate action-level results connect normalized self-current to count-scaled frequencies, conserved standing-wave energy and reciprocal cross-depth response. These results motivate a common physical explanation, with their additional premises made explicit. They do not yet provide one action selecting all observed particles or explain the absence of higher-sector strong forces. The paper presents the mathematical connections, their scope and concrete spectral and interaction tests.

The latest constructions extend that reuse: one spatial band supplies contact, kinetic dressing and transport; the geometric color rank fixes pair factors and conditional charge fractions; directed angular energies give exact shape spectra. A finite sawtooth preparation also tests nearly equal charged-lepton response and action-dependent depth-five suppression with a common receiver. These are linked conditional results, with waveform occupation and the physical interaction still to be justified.

1. The Scientific Question

A useful organizing principle earns attention when it continues to constrain new questions. If a proposed spatial structure helps organize masses, the next test is whether the same structure can also accommodate the particles' rotational and interaction properties without acquiring a separate adjustable rule for every observation.

That is the question pursued here. IDWT associates particle families with depths in one nested spatial manifold. The empirical starting point is a combinatorial mass pattern. The further motivation is that the same candidate depths support explicit mathematics relevant to other properties. The research opportunity is to determine whether these pieces follow from one physical law.

The case for investigation is the combination of numerical restriction and reusable geometry. Neither requires claiming that the full theory is complete. Both can be examined now, with explicit equations and reproducible comparisons.

The proposed chain is physically definite: spatial patterns have a spectrum; their geometry constrains rotation and phase; the same field's response produces contact and changes those patterns. A three-dimensional observer registers that response. The task is to connect these steps through one action, rather than independently adjusting them for each particle.

Six results give a short route into the argument:

  • Rigid mass-frequencies: the shared count law has large rung gaps and a unique complete depth arrangement at the existing individual accuracies under its specified scale recipe.
  • Orbit and observer geometry: one six-dimensional generator and a stated readout produce an entire petal sequence.
  • Spectra and spin together: one specified connection on compatible six-/ten-dimensional spatial geometries supplies both count-polynomial identities and available observer half-spin states.
  • The quark-depth distinction: complete middle-Hodge channels have rank three only at depths three and four. A second test agrees on a minimal spinor branch, but fails on the full paired carrier.
  • Charge, handedness and frames: depth five gives a neutral handed channel under a chosen generator; a separate six-normal construction supplies the relative charge table and compatible spatial frames and contact tensors.
  • Action and response bridges: a local normalized-current construction constrains the count-to-frequency mechanism; spatial overlap, canonical normalization and a common interaction energy give explicit reciprocal responses.

The mass comparisons test a numerical proposal against measurements. The geometric and action results are conditional mathematics. Their combined value is that a common explanation must satisfy these constraints together. Shared premises are explanatory reuse, not independent statistical evidence.

What a Sector Means

The depth ddd counts ordinary spatial dimensions of the same kind as the familiar three. Sectors form one nested chain in an infinite-dimensional physical manifold. The proposed electron sector has six such dimensions; the tau sector has ten. Sector inclusion does not make an electron a constituent of a tau. Particle patterns remain distinct, and their orientations need not define a universal fixed grid.

Mass is expressed in equivalent frequency units,

ωm=mc2ℏ. \omega_m=\frac{mc^2}{\hbar}. ωm​=ℏmc2​.

The model seeks the dynamics selecting that frequency. Physical field amplitude is not identified with mass; it remains unspecified where it cancels and must be retained where nonlinear dynamics makes it relevant.

and therefore

The scale has disappeared. Using the archived electron mass to evaluate the shared scale gives a muon mass of 105.656547603 MeV/c2c^2c2, against the archived benchmark 105.6583755 MeV/c2c^2c2: a signed residual of approximately −0.00173001%-0.00173001\%−0.00173001%, or −17.3-17.3−17.3 parts per million. Both particles are higher harmonics of the same sector fundamental; the electron is the calibration reference, not that fundamental.

The exact adjacent-rung identities explain how restrictive the comparison is:

S(n+1,d)−S(n,d)S(n,d)=dn,S(n,d)−S(n−1,d)S(n,d)=dn+d−1. \frac{S(n+1,d)-S(n,d)}{S(n,d)}=\frac dn, \qquad \frac{S(n,d)-S(n-1,d)}{S(n,d)}=\frac d{n+d-1}. S(n,d)S(n+1,d)−S(n,d)​=nd​,S(n,d)S(n,d)−S(n−1,d)​=n+d−1d​.

At the muon assignment, stepping down changes the count by 15%; stepping up changes it by approximately 17.1429%. The observed residual is about 8,700 times smaller than the smaller of those steps. Moving the muon index by one cannot supply a small repair. Adjusting the sector scale also moves the electron.

This is the sense in which the formula is rigid. The 8,700 comparison is a measure of local rung spacing relative to error, not a chance probability or a measure of experimental significance. The 17.3-parts-per-million discrepancy is much larger than the measurement uncertainty, so the uncorrected count ratio is not an exact mass law. It is a precise target for a dynamical explanation or a principled correction.

What Is Being Counted?

The count has a standard, explicit meaning:

S(n,d)=∑k=0n−1(k+d−1d−1)=#{(a0,…,ad)∈Nd+1:∑j=0daj=n−1}. S(n,d)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\binom{k+d-1}{d-1} =\#\left\{(a_0,\ldots,a_d)\in\mathbb N^{d+1}: \sum_{j=0}^{d}a_j=n-1\right\}. S(n,d)=k=0∑n−1​(d−1k+d−1​)=#{(a0​,…,ad​)∈Nd+1:j=0∑d​aj​=n−1}.

It counts oscillator configurations through total excitation n−1n-1n−1, equivalently monomials of degree at most n−1n-1n−1 in ddd variables. The extra coordinate is a slack variable, not an additional physical dimension. The sum is the Hockey-Stick Identity, and adjacent counts obey Pascal recursion:

S(n,d)=S(n,d−1)+S(n−1,d). S(n,d)=S(n,d-1)+S(n-1,d). S(n,d)=S(n,d−1)+S(n−1,d).

Thus the mass proposal uses an established count of available configurations. In IDWT's law this count is exactly the proposed frequency multiplier: ωn,d=ω0,dS(n,d)\omega_{n,d}=\omega_{0,d}S(n,d)ωn,d​=ω0,d​S(n,d), with ω0,d=μdc2/ℏ\omega_{0,d}=\mu_dc^2/\hbarω0,d​=μd​c2/ℏ. The open spectral problem is which spatial operator and same-field dynamics produce this frequency spectrum and select the occupied rungs. The combinatorial count identifies the target spectrum; the operator must explain it.

A Complete Assignment Test with Every Positive Integer Index

The stronger comparison has now been carried out. It exchanges five intact blocks—W/Z/H, down/strange/bottom, up/charm/top, electron/muon and tau—among the five depths with specified absolute scales, {2,3,4,6,10}\{2,3,4,6,10\}{2,3,4,6,10}. Different blocks must occupy distinct depths. Every observed mass stays fixed, including the electron, and the numerical scale prescription in Appendix A and the shared charged-lepton unit remain unchanged. Tau's separate block reflects its proposed sector, not a different empirical lepton family.

Among all 120 complete permutations, only the maintained arrangement matches or improves every particle's existing mass accuracy. Unlike the fixed-index table above, this test permits every positive integer index. It has no arbitrary upper cutoff: strict growth of S(n,d)S(n,d)S(n,d) lets exact rational comparisons identify the globally nearest rung from the two neighboring values around each target mass. Increasing an index beyond those neighbors cannot repair an excluded arrangement.

The electron and tau are allowed to change sectors in the enumeration. The unchanged reference equation admits 24 permutations; requiring the two lepton sectors to share their unit leaves six. The other five complete arrangements all fail at least one existing individual accuracy, even at their best possible integer choices.

The explicit uniqueness theorems now provide a direct proof. Under the same reference and scale constraints, even allowing a 0.5% W error and a 100% up-quark error forces this depth arrangement. Exact gaps between adjacent rungs exclude the other placements. A second theorem proves that matching every original individual logarithmic accuracy fixes all twelve integer indices uniquely as well, including bottom's comparison rung. The proof covers every positive integer and uses exact rational inequalities.

The physical meaning is the simultaneous restriction. An isolated improvement obtained by moving down-type quarks into depth six does not supply a complete alternative when electron/muon must also have a sector of their own. A competing arrangement must satisfy the reference equation, common scales and every remaining mass comparison together. Under the specified prescription, only the current arrangement reaches the current individual accuracies.

This strengthens the case for investigating the sector structure conditional on its numerical scale recipe. The reference factor already contains the electron count 18564, so recovering the electron's assigned depth and index is consistency with that input, not another independent prediction. The test does not derive the scale coefficients, select occupied modes dynamically or establish uniqueness across other scale laws. Depth five's absolute neutrino scale and the massless photon are outside this positive-mass comparison.

The complete assignment result publishes the proof, fixed mass inputs, all six admissible arrangements, classifications of all 120 permutations and runnable calculations. It also retains the broader normalization controls and a separately scoped finite reference-null calculation. The uniqueness result itself requires no claim of zero probability or astronomical discovery odds.

Its full ray space has real dimension 2m−22^m-22m−2; its pure-spinor orbit has dimension m(m−1)m(m-1)m(m−1). Equating either with the spatial dimension 2m2m2m selects m=3m=3m=3. This is a precise reason to examine the proposed six-dimensional geometry. The two equalities reflect the same representation structure and reinforce its coherence; they are not two independent experimental observations.

This is distinct from statistical independence. Several consequences of one representation can make that representation more useful without being several independent measurements. No product of coincidence probabilities is assigned here.

8. The Research Problems That Could Change the Assessment

The useful next contributions have definite inputs and outcomes. They need not solve the whole theory at once.

A. Test the Numerical Organizing Principle More Severely

Reproduce the complete assignment test in section 3, then extend its declared scope: examine measurement uncertainties and quark mass conventions, and compare justified alternative scale laws or state-selection mechanisms. Keep the existing reference, shared-scale and exclusive-depth constraints when testing the maintained prescription; label any relaxed comparison. The published uniqueness result covers all positive integer indices within that prescription. It leaves the historical selection of the coefficients and law uncalibrated. A controlled alternative with comparable simplicity and accuracy would weaken the case.

B. Derive the Spatial Frequency Spectrum

Use spectral geometry as the central tool: specify the spatial operator, its metric and connection, self-adjoint domain and boundary or asymptotic conditions across the nested sectors. IDWT's target is the spectrum ωn,d=ω0,dS(n,d)\omega_{n,d}=\omega_{0,d}S(n,d)ωn,d​=ω0,d​S(n,d). Start from the explicit spectral families in section 5 or the local-current bridge in section 7, or a justified alternative, and derive one kinetic and self-interaction law whose complete particle clock has that spectrum. Keep operator eigenvalues, multiplicities and integrated counts defined separately within the derivation, and show the mechanism relating them. Account for the spatial Dirac contribution, support energy and sector scale. The observed electron–muon residual fixes the direction and size of a correction to test; an arbitrary independent correction per particle would give up the formula's central restriction.

C. Select the Occupied States

Determine whether one nonlinear or geometric mechanism selects the maintained indices and spin-one-half branches while treating the additional states consistently. The existing quadratic projective law leaves observer-spin components degenerate, providing a concrete starting obstruction. A successful extension must show how the degeneracy changes and why the relevant states persist. Count availability alone does not answer occupation.

D. Complete the Orbit and Observer Construction

Derive the preparation and observer response of section 4 from a supported electron–nucleus configuration. Compare actual spatial densities, angular observables and spectra, including the L=0L=0L=0 case. The present generator and robust petal count give a reproducible starting calculation; matching their silhouette alone would leave the physical identification unresolved.

E. Derive Reciprocal Coupling from the Same Field

Calculate interactions with each particle retaining its own isolated frequency and an evolving relative phase. Include the polarization of both participants, their responding spatial shapes, supporting stress and conserved energy–momentum. Recover the common charged-lepton response while testing the proposed neutral handed channel. Use depths two, three and four alongside five, six and ten as controls under the same law; a depth-five effect must be distinguished from a generic odd-dimensional effect. This would connect the sector geometry to a measurable interaction law.

F. Test the Common Geometric Premises

Compare the universal alternating-frame rule with weaker polarization requirements and alternative normal dimensions. Within the compatible spatial examples, determine which charge carriers, global spin sections and contact maps remain compatible with the actual Levi–Civita operator. The round and nonspin controls already distinguish normal parallelness, ambient Clifford closure and one contact's blindness to determinant curvature. The complete monogenic classification gives a further exact test: a projected doublet can vanish where its full charge-triplet section does not. A proposed geometric interaction rule should state which of those quantities it uses. These questions can be addressed without requiring particle simulations or completing the mass dynamics first.

G. Derive Color and Its Absence Elsewhere

Test the complete three/four Hodge channels as equivalent spatial modes under one field law. Derive an SU(3)SU(3)SU(3) response commuting with observed spin, rather than identifying a rotation triple with color. Justify any minimal-carrier projection. Apply the same interaction and occupation prescription at depths two, five, six and ten and neighboring controls. In particular, show why allowed higher-rank quartic response or non-Abelian curvature does not create additional strong forces. The rank-three criterion and a possible determinant vertex are starting constraints, not that missing force-absence proof.

H. Derive the Harmonic Source and Its Readout

Keep the supplied mass-frequency endpoint and distinguish the spatial shell cutoff from the temporal harmonic cutoff. Derive which modes are occupied and whether integrated density, local evaluation or another spatial source reads their interference. Determine whether the same-field reduction gives density coupling, velocity-source coupling or both, including moving orientation and unequal sector clocks. Use the exact Fourier coefficients and receiver tail bounds to compare all maintained sectors under the same law. This tests whether the nearly equal charged-lepton response and conditional depth-five suppression survive a physical action, rather than adopting a derivative merely to obtain the latter.

These questions call on spectral geometry, nonlinear Dirac equations, representation theory, constrained stability and particle phenomenology. Each offers a way to improve or reject a specific part of the proposal. The linked derivations and executable comparisons make it possible to contribute without accepting every IDWT premise.

9. Conclusion

The case is a convergence of constraints on one proposed spatial classification. Its numerical foundation is the restrictive mass-frequency law: under the stated scale prescription and simultaneous family constraints, only the maintained complete assignment reaches every existing individual accuracy over all positive integer indices. Its geometric development goes beyond masses. The same assigned depths enter orbit morphology, spectral and half-spin compatibility, a depth-five handed neutral channel and two conditional three/four channel criteria relevant to color.

Further mathematics begins connecting those properties to interaction. One compatible normal geometry links charge weights, frames, spin sections and contact tensors. A separate local-current action constrains how the count-scaled clock can arise and supplies exact standing-wave energy and flux identities. Spatial marginals and canonical kinetic metrics give reciprocal response and a consistent way to compare charges and vertices across depths. Actual spatial-band evaluation now links counts, contact, transport and kinetic dressing. The same color rank fixes pair factors and conditional charge fractions; angular energies give exact response spectra. A finite harmonic preparation adds a common cross-sector coupling comparison with explicit density-versus-derivative action choices. These are explicit bridges to the proposed picture of particles as interacting resonant spatial patterns.

The outstanding task is a common physical realization. The construction must justify its carriers and operator, select occupied states and sector scales, retain complete energy–momentum and reproduce interaction observables. Color also requires the absence of analogous higher-sector strong forces. The current results make these tests more specific; they do not settle them.

The sector structure merits independent investigation because it combines a restrictive frequency pattern with reusable mathematical connections to other particle properties. A successful common law would explain several constraints together. The linked proofs, comparisons and executable checks permit that possibility to be assessed directly.

Appendix D. Reproduce or Extend the Calculations

The mass program, sector comparison script and recorded comparison results reproduce the mass ratios, scale diagnostics and rung gaps. The reviewed sector checks and their results check the additional count polynomials, angular multiplicities, nesting and normal-mode arithmetic. Their inputs are explicit archived benchmarks; algebraic checks do not substitute for tests of physical premises.

The unified charge-geometry script and its recorded results reproduce the exterior representations, induced connection, normal-rank comparison, allowed charge alternatives and tangent/normal occupation tests in section 7. Run the one script with Python and installed SymPy; it creates a new dated results directory. Its 355 exact checks include 168 selector/depth cases and a bounded integer-character comparison. The charge-geometry results concern stated geometric hypotheses and do not supply a four-of-six-sector preference.

The shared geometry checker and its results reproduce the new normal-frame, common-carrier, curvature, contact and alternative-dimension controls. The all-dimension and global claims also require the proofs in the linked shared-normal-geometry note; finite checks alone do not establish those theorems.

The color-depth checker and recorded results contain 36,489 exact checks of the uniform Hodge and rotation-Casimir channels, full-carrier controls, projected-mode algebra and higher-sector response. The normal-charge checker and results give the rotation-alignment, character and oriented-volume controls. Check counts describe executed comparisons, not the strength of physical evidence. The all-dimensional conclusions require the accompanying proofs.

The spatial-band integration checker and results preserve 2,529 checks of counts, contact projectors, kinetic dressing, color contractions, charge consistency and angular Hessians. Spatial and angular comparisons cover 2 through 12; the geometric color/parity comparison covers 2 through 16. The sawtooth checker and results add 2,023 checks of exact Fourier identities, reciprocal phase averages, unequal-clock encounters, canonical source transformations and the common all-sector receiver. Both reports identify the executed source hashes. Check counts describe verification coverage, not empirical evidential weight.

The local-current, coherent-overlap, canonical-normalization and reciprocity notes linked in section 7 contain their derivations and source-pinned checkers. Their hypotheses differ from one another where stated; no result is transferred to another action merely because both use the same sector depth.

The complete assignment study supplies the exact unbounded-index proof, full permutation results and portable scripts. Its separate finite reference-null results retain their stated cutoff and are not odds for the uncapped proof.

External mathematics is used with stated scope: critical flat Dirac profiles with their exponent; projective Dirac eigenfamilies with their metric and line convention; and ordinary tensor representations with a specified observer restriction. These sources provide tools for the calculations, not endorsements of the particle assignments.

For a focused contribution, choose one question in section 8, retain the listed inputs, and state which new assumptions the proposed result needs. A successful calculation should show both what it explains and what else the same law predicts. A negative result should identify the precise construction it excludes. Either can determine whether the sector pattern is the beginning of a common physical explanation.
